decisions.topic: Channel count: hard-wired 4 vs parameterized N
options: Fixed 4 channels
Parameter NUM_BUTTONS, default 4
decisions.choice: Parameter NUM_BUTTONS with default 4. Each channel is an identical, independent instance of the per-button logic.
decisions.rationale: The spec says four buttons. A width parameter costs nothing and lets the same block serve later panel revisions.
decisions.question: Should the block be fixed at exactly 4 buttons, or parameterized on button count with 4 as the default?

done_when: The Overview names the four stages in order: synchronizer, polarity inversion, debounce filter, edge detector.
The Overview states the three outputs per button: level, press pulse, release pulse.
The Overview states the scope: no interrupt or bus interface, and outputs are consumed in the same clock domain.

steps.title: Build-time parameters for clock frequency and debounce time, and the derived count
steps.goal: Define the parameters that let the user retarget from 50 MHz to 100 MHz and change the ~10 ms window without editing RTL. Define the derived terminal count and counter width.

spec_evidence.quote: around 10 ms is what our hardware guy suggests
able to change that when we build the bitstream
The board clock is 50 MHz today, but the next
revision will be 100 MHz, so please don't hard-code it.

options: CLK_FREQ_HZ + DEBOUNCE_MS parameters, count derived
CLK_FREQ_HZ + DEBOUNCE_US parameters, count derived
Single DEBOUNCE_CYCLES parameter computed by the integrator
decisions.choice: Two Verilog parameters: clock frequency in Hz and debounce time. The terminal count is CLK_FREQ_HZ*time/scale, computed at elaboration, with counter width from $clog2. Defaults are 50_000_000 Hz and 10 ms.
decisions.rationale: The spec explicitly asks for a build-time debounce time and for the clock not to be hard-coded.

options: Milliseconds (integer)
Microseconds (integer)
decisions.choice: Microseconds (DEBOUNCE_US, default 10000). This gives sub-ms tuning while the derived count stays an exact integer at 50 and 100 MHz.
decisions.rationale: The spec only says 'around 10 ms'. Microseconds allow values like 5.5 ms without fractional parameters.
decisions.question: Is it OK to specify the debounce time in microseconds (e.g. 10000 for 10 ms), or do you want a milliseconds parameter?

done_when: The parameter table lists name, default, unit, and legal range for clock frequency, debounce time, and button count.
The derived terminal-count formula is written out, with worked values for 50 MHz and 100 MHz at 10 ms (500000 and 1000000).
Counter width is derived with $clog2 and is shown to be 19 or 20 bits for those cases.
Integer-overflow risk in the elaboration-time multiply is addressed, e.g. by ordering the division or using 64-bit localparam math.

options: Invert after the synchronizer, so all internal state is 1 = pressed
Keep internal state active-low and invert only at the outputs
decisions.choice: Invert immediately after the synchronizer. All internal state and every output use 1 = pressed.
decisions.rationale: The spec requires outputs where 1 = pressed. Inverting early keeps the debounce and edge logic in one polarity and puts no logic between the pin and the first sync flop.

options: Three NUM_BUTTONS-wide vectors (level, pressed pulse, released pulse)
Single level vector plus combined event vector with type bit
decisions.choice: Three separate NUM_BUTTONS-wide output vectors: debounced level, press pulse, release pulse.
decisions.rationale: The spec asks for a level plus a pulse on press and a pulse on release. Separate vectors map directly onto those requests and onto firmware register bits.
decisions.question: Are three per-button output vectors (level, press pulse, release pulse) the right shape, or do you need a different packing for your firmware interface?

done_when: The port table gives name, direction, width, polarity, and clock domain for every port.
The raw inputs are explicitly marked asynchronous and active-low.

steps.title: Metastability-safe input synchronizer per button
steps.goal: Specify the multi-flop synchronizer on each raw pin and its MTBF rationale. Rule out any logic before the first flop and any fan-out from the first stage.

spec_evidence.quote: these pins are obviously not synchronized to anything
Our last vendor's design had metastability problems.

options: 2-flop
3-flop
Parameter SYNC_STAGES default 2
decisions.choice: Parameter SYNC_STAGES with default 2 and minimum 2. The flops carry ASYNC_REG/keep attributes so they are placed adjacent.
decisions.rationale: Two flops are standard at 50-100 MHz, and slow mechanical inputs give a large MTBF. The parameter lets the user add a third stage, given the vendor's previous metastability history.
decisions.question: Is a 2-flop synchronizer (configurable to 3) acceptable, or do you require 3 stages by policy?

done_when: The synchronizer chain is drawn with no combinational logic before stage 1.
The MA notes the synthesis attributes (ASYNC_REG or equivalent) and a timing-constraint note (false path or set_max_delay on pin-to-first-flop).
The MA states that only the last sync stage feeds the inverter and the debouncer.
The synchronizer reset value corresponds to 'not pressed' (raw = 1).

steps.title: Debounce filter: stability counter and debounced state register
steps.goal: Define the per-channel algorithm. The debounced level changes only after the synchronized, inverted input has differed from the current level continuously for the configured time. Decide the counter organization.

spec_evidence.quote: for each button, a clean level signal that only changes after the button has
been stable for a while, around 10 ms is what our hardware guy suggests

options: Restart counter on any mismatch; flip state when counter hits terminal count (continuous stable-window)
Periodic sampling at debounce interval (sample-and-compare)
Saturating up/down integrator
decisions.choice: Continuous stable-window. While the synced input equals the current debounced state the counter is held at 0. While they differ the counter increments. On reaching the terminal count the state flips and the counter clears.
decisions.rationale: This matches 'only changes after the button has been stable for a while' exactly. It is deterministic, and its latency bound is easy to verify.
decisions.question: Should the output change only after the input has been continuously stable for the full debounce time (any bounce restarts the timer), or is a periodic-sampling/integrating filter acceptable?

options: Independent full-width counter per button
Shared prescaler tick (e.g. 1 kHz or 1 MHz) plus small per-button counters
decisions.choice: Independent full-width counter per button, counting clock cycles.
decisions.rationale: This gives exact timing and the simplest verification. At 4 channels × ~20 bits the area is trivial. A shared prescaler adds up to one tick of timing jitter and couples the channels.
decisions.question: Is a full-resolution counter per button acceptable (≈20 flops each), or would you prefer a shared prescaler with small per-button counters to save area at the cost of ±1 tick timing?

done_when: The per-channel datapath is drawn: sync output -> inverter -> comparator vs state -> counter -> terminal-count compare -> state register.
The counter update rules are given as a truth table (match, mismatch, terminal).
The MA states the counter never wraps and its width covers the terminal count.
The block diagram shows NUM_BUTTONS replicated channels sharing only clk and reset.

steps.title: Press/release one-clock pulse generation from debounced state
steps.goal: Derive the press and release pulses from transitions of the debounced state so each physical press yields exactly one press pulse and one release pulse, each exactly one clock wide.

spec_evidence.quote: The firmware also really only cares about the moment a button is pressed and the moment it's

decisions.topic: Pulse timing relative to level change
options: Registered pulse asserted in the same cycle the debounced level register changes
Pulse from delayed-copy edge detect (one cycle after level changes)
Combinational pulse from the terminal-count condition
decisions.choice: Registered pulses set in the same clock edge that flips the debounced level, i.e. press_q <= flip & ~state and release_q <= flip & state. This keeps level and pulses aligned and glitch-free.
decisions.rationale: Firmware sees the level and the event coincide. All outputs come straight from flops.
decisions.question: Is it acceptable that the press/release pulse is asserted in the same clock cycle the debounced level changes, rather than one cycle after?

done_when: The pulse equations are written in terms of the flip condition and the current state.
The MA guarantees a pulse width of exactly 1 cycle and no back-to-back pulses on one channel within one debounce time.
The MA states that press and release can never be asserted simultaneously on the same channel.

steps.goal: Document the cycle-accurate latency from a stable raw pin change to the level and pulse outputs, and the timing-critical path (counter increment and compare).

done_when: Latency is expressed as SYNC_STAGES + terminal count + register stages, with numeric values at 50 and 100 MHz.
A timing diagram shows a bouncing press, the counter restarts, the level change, and the press pulse.

steps.title: Reset strategy for the active-low global reset and power-up state
steps.goal: Define how rst_n is applied to the sync flops, counters, state, and pulse registers, and what outputs look like coming out of reset.

spec_evidence.quote: There's a global reset coming from our reset controller, active-low.

options: Asynchronous assert, synchronous deassert assumed from reset controller
Fully synchronous reset
Asynchronous reset with internal reset synchronizer in this block
decisions.choice: Asynchronous active-low reset on all flops. Deassertion is assumed to be already synchronized to clk by the external reset controller, and no internal reset synchronizer is added.
decisions.rationale: A dedicated reset controller usually provides synchronized release. Async assert guarantees defined outputs even without a running clock.
decisions.question: Is the active-low reset from your reset controller already synchronized to this block's clock on deassertion, and do you prefer asynchronous or synchronous reset flops?

decisions.topic: Debounced state after reset when a button is held
options: Reset to 'released'; a held button produces a press pulse after one debounce time
Initialize from the input after reset, with no pulse for buttons held at reset
decisions.choice: Reset all debounced levels to 0 (released) and sync flops to the idle pin value. A button held through reset is reported as a normal press, with a pulse, one debounce time after reset release.
decisions.rationale: This is simple and deterministic, and firmware learns of held buttons through the normal path. Suppressing the pulse would need extra startup logic.
decisions.question: If a button is held down while reset is released, should firmware get a press pulse once it's debounced, or should the block silently start in the pressed state?

done_when: The MA lists the reset value of every register class (sync, counter, state, pulse).
The single clock domain is stated, with the raw pins as the only asynchronous inputs.

The MA states that outputs are 0 during reset.
